reader.title: Tarring and feathering of Andrew Elliott
chips: Lynching of any race (not in the anti-Black count)
bases: A group calling itself or called a vigilance committee seized Elliott at night, threatened him with hanging and tarred and feathered him; no one was killed (A2, A13, A5).
Several men acting without legal authority punished Elliott for an alleged offense and threatened to hang him, but he was tarred and feathered and survived, so no one was killed (A2, A5, A13).

The Globe telegram, the Benton dispatch, the Dakotaian and Barbour briefs and the Oct. 30 follow-up independently agree that Elliott was taken at night and tarred and feathered at Grand Forks (A2, A4, A5, A8, A13).

summary.text: The tarring and feathering of Andrew Elliott was a night attack at Grand Forks, Dakota Territory, in late October 1882, in which a 'vigilance committee' seized a man accused of exposing himself to school girls, threatened to hang him, and covered him with tar and feathers.
Elliott survived, and within days Grand Forks dispatches reported that townspeople doubted his guilt and called the affair an outrage.

According to a Grand Forks dispatch printed in the Benton Weekly Record, a man calling himself Dr. Andrew Elliott had been in the town for about a week 'without visible means of support' and was often drunk.
The same dispatch accused him of exposing himself to Mrs. L. Lamb, the wife of a real estate dealer, and of loitering near the schoolhouse, and said her husband 'laid his plans' to punish him.
Both the Benton dispatch and a special telegram to the St. Paul Daily Globe said he then exposed himself to school girls and made indecent proposals.
About two o'clock in the morning, a group described by the Globe as 'several determined men' took Elliott from his bed at the Griggs House.
In the Globe's account they walked him to the railroad bridge where a man named Thurber, called 'the ravisher', had been hanged, and told him he had only a short time to live.
Under that threat, the Globe said, he partly confessed while denying that he had meant to force the girl.
The men took him to 'a quiet spot', stripped him and covered him with tar and feathers, and the Benton dispatch said the little girl identified him.
He was turned loose, and the Yankton Press and Dakotaian reported that he had been left in the woods and might die from exposure.

A Grand Forks dispatch of Oct. 30, printed in the Bismarck Tribune and the Jamestown Weekly Alert, said Elliott had been found at East Grand Forks 'very low' and that a committee of doctors had attended him.
He denied having made any confession, and the dispatch said people in Grand Forks generally denounced the affair as an outrage, holding 'a strong belief' in his innocence.
No report of arrests or prosecution of the men appears in the coverage.
Only white papers covered the episode, and none of them mentioned Elliott's race.
The Globe headed its telegram with a joke about a man 'Treated to a Valuable New Dress', and the Benton dispatch called him 'the wretch' and spoke of a 'full fall suit of tar and feathers'.
Dakota papers took a different line in the follow-up, which the Bismarck Tribune headed 'Bad Break for Grand Forks' and listed as 'Too Much Justice at Grand Forks'.

In November a short miscellany paragraph ran in papers from Virginia to Nevada, saying a mob had taken Elliott out of jail and put a rope round his neck before he talked them down to tar and feathers.
A separate Kansas brief, also reprinted, described him as 'obnoxious' for advances to school girls and said he was later found on the Minnesota side of the river in a terrible condition.
The jail-and-rope version conflicts with the Grand Forks-datelined accounts, which place the seizure at the Griggs House and describe the hanging only as a threat at the bridge.
The Grand Forks dispatches are closer to the event and more detailed, while the jail version appears only in a distant, undated paragraph.
The confession rests on the attackers' account in the Globe, and Elliott later denied making it.

accounts.label: Globe special telegram
accounts.gist: Men took Elliott from bed at the Griggs House, threatened him at the bridge where Thurber was hanged until he partly confessed, then tarred and feathered him; next morning some felt he was not guilty.

accounts.label: Benton dispatch (Grand Forks, Oct. 28)
accounts.gist: A vagrant 'Dr.' Elliott, accused of exposing himself to Mrs. Lamb and to a girl, was taken from bed by a vigilance committee at 2 a.m., identified by the girl and tarred and feathered.

accounts.label: Oct. 30 follow-up
accounts.gist: Elliott was found at East Grand Forks very low, denied confessing, and townspeople called the affair an outrage.

accounts.label: Jail-and-rope paragraph
accounts.gist: A mob took Elliott out of jail and put a rope round his neck, but he talked them down to tar and feathers.

framing.detail: The Globe headlined a man 'Treated to a Valuable New Dress' yet reported a feeling he was not guilty.
The Benton dispatch called Elliott 'the wretch' and described the tarring as a 'full fall suit'.
The Dakota follow-up, headed 'Bad Break for Grand Forks' and 'Too Much Justice at Grand Forks', reported the town calling it an outrage.
The jail-and-rope paragraph ran as a light miscellany item in Virginia, Nevada and other papers.
